extracted.intended_audience: practitioners before the USPTO and parties to USPTO disciplinary proceedings (OED, respondents, counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria used in USPTO disciplinary proceedings to determine whether a practitioner violated USPTO rules and what sanction is appropriate, including burdens of proof, enumerated rule violations, discovery and procedural compliance expectations, and sanctioning factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO authority to regulate practice and impose discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO has the exclusive authority to establish qualifications for admitting persons to practice before it, and to suspend or exclude them from practicing before it. The Director may suspend or exclude a person shown to be incompetent, disreputable, guilty of gross misconduct, or who violates Office regulations. Practitioner must receive notice and opportunity for a hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory and regulatory citations: 35 U.S.C. § 32; 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.39, 11.44. Disciplinary hearings conducted under USPTO rules and section 7 of the APA, 5 U.S.C. § 556, by an impartial hearing officer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof — clear and convincing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence; the respondent bears the burden to prove any affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited rule: 37 C.F.R. § 11.49. Clear and convincing is an intermediate standard between preponderance and beyond a reasonable doubt and requires evidence producing a firm belief or conviction in the trier of fact (Addington v. Texas; Jimenez v. DaimlerChrysler).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'clear and convincing' standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The clear and convincing standard requires evidence 'of such weight that it produces in the mind of the trier of fact a firm belief or conviction, without hesitancy, as to the truth of the allegations sought to be established.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence is 'clear' if certain, unambiguous, and plain; 'convincing' if reasonable and persuasive enough to cause belief (Foster v. Allied Signal; Ortega v. IBP). Used to protect important liberty interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to respond to lawful requests for information (37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner fails to respond to lawful OED RFIs if they provide non-responsive, evasive, incomplete, or materially false answers to requests for information and supporting documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include answering 'see attached' but attaching misleading documents, promising documentation and never providing it, or otherwise ignoring required documentary support. Violations can be proven by showing intentional or evasive responses (citing cases: In re Chaobal, Bender v. Dudas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5) / § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Misconduct includes conduct which impedes or subverts dispute resolution or frustrates the fair balance of interests essential to litigation or other proceedings; it harms public perception or confidence in the courts or legal profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Does not require a mental state beyond negligence. Examples: failure to file tax returns, refusal to pay court-ordered judgments, making false statements to tribunals, providing evasive responses to RFIs. Cited authorities include In re Friedman; Att’y Grievance Comm’n v. Rand; In re Martinez.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner engages in misconduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation by knowingly making false statements or submitting altered or fabricated evidence to tribunals or disciplinary bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material misrepresentations that impact central issues, cause delay or waste resources, or are intended to deceive support a finding of this violation (citing cases such as Custis, Ogunmeno).

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowingly making false statements to tribunals (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a violation for a practitioner to make knowingly false statements of fact to a tribunal, including disciplinary boards or bankruptcy courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextual examples include falsely certifying no unsatisfied judgments or timely filed tax returns on a reinstatement questionnaire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowingly disobeying obligations under the rules of a tribunal (37 C.F.R. § 11.304(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner violates the rule by knowingly failing to obey tribunal rules or court orders (e.g., refusing to pay judgments, failing to comply with discovery orders).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated disobedience or refusal to comply supports sanctioning, including potential exclusion; examples include failing to pay multiple judgments and failing to comply with arbitrator/court orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal conduct reflecting adversely on fitness (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Criminal acts (or conduct reaching the level of criminality) that adversely reflect on a practitioner's honesty, trustworthiness, or fitness to practice are sanctionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to timely pay federal taxes may constitute criminal conduct reflecting adversely on fitness; cited rule 11.804(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery obligations and sanctions (including preclusion and adverse inference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must adequately answer interrogatories and produce responsive documents in discovery; evasive conduct (e.g., 'document dump' without identification) can lead to sanctions such as preclusion from offering documentary evidence and adverse inferences that withheld answers would have been damaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunal may compel adequate responses, set deadlines, strike improper supplements, and preclude evidence or draw adverse inferences when a party acts in bad faith or repeatedly fails to comply with discovery orders (Ruling on Fourth Motion to Compel and for Sanctions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and compliance with filing rules and page/format limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Filings must comply with established deadlines, page limits, and formatting requirements; attempts to circumvent page limits (e.g., inserting arguments as exhibits, footnotes that contain extended argument, oversized tables) will be stricken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunal may strike late or non-compliant supplements and deny leave to refile when filings are prepared with intent to circumvent rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely and sufficiently pled objections to hearing exhibits (objection waiver)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections to opposing party exhibits must be timely raised and sufficiently pleaded so the Tribunal can discern the basis; untimely or insufficiently pled objections are deemed waived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunal admonished that an objection not timely raised or insufficiently pled will be waived; failure to timely object may result in admission of exhibits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-hearing exhibit exchange obligations and sanctions for failure to exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties are required to exchange hearing exhibits by the deadlines; failure to timely exchange exhibits can result in sanction precluding the noncompliant party from producing any evidence at the hearing (subject to limited impeachment exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunal may authorize limited impeachment evidence, but general failure to comply supports exclusion of exhibits and potentially witnesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity issues and use of expert testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: When authenticity of evidence (e.g., emails) is contested, the Tribunal may require expert witness testimony to determine authenticity and may keep the record open to receive such testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impeachment evidence must meet the Tribunal's standard; fabricated exhibits or improperly offered impeachment materials may be rejected and can support findings of dishonesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning framework (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)) — four factors to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Before imposing discipline, the Tribunal must consider: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused; and (4) the existence of aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The primary purpose of attorney discipline is protection of the public and the bar, not punishment. The Tribunal looks to ABA Standards for imposing lawyer sanctions for guidance (In re Burmeister, Coombs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental state definitions and culpability (intentional vs knowing vs negligent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intentional conduct arises when a lawyer acts with a conscious objective to accomplish a result; 'knowing' is acting with conscious awareness of the nature or attendant circumstances of conduct without necessarily having a conscious objective; negligence is a lesser mental state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mental-state findings affect sanction severity; intentional and knowing misconduct are more culpable and weigh heavily toward exclusion when combined with other factors (citing In re Glazer and In re Aquilla definitions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating and mitigating factors to be weighed
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal considers aggravating factors (dishonest/selfish motive; pattern of misconduct/multiple offenses; bad-faith obstruction of the disciplinary process; substantial experience as a practitioner; indifference to restitution; refusal to acknowledge wrongdoing) and mitigating factors (e.g., absence of prior disciplinary record).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunal often consults ABA Standards to identify and weigh these factors. Multiple aggravating factors and few mitigators support more severe sanctions, possibly exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of actual or potential injury
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions analysis includes assessing the amount of actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner's misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: unpaid taxes and unpaid judgments that caused financial injury to creditors and required them to expend resources to enforce judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary purpose of discipline — protection of the public and bar
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering sanctions, the Tribunal starts from the premise that protecting the public and the bar, not punishment, is the primary purpose of attorney discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This premise guides the balancing of aggravating and mitigating factors and selection of appropriate sanction (cited: In re Burmeister; Coombs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible sanction of exclusion and duties while excluded (37 C.F.R. § 11.58)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal may order exclusion (suspension/exclusion from practice before the USPTO) as a sanction for severe misconduct; excluded practitioners have specific duties while excluded under 37 C.F.R. § 11.58.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusion is appropriate when misconduct is intentional, involves lying, causes actual injury, and aggravating factors predominate; the Tribunal may direct the excluded practitioner to duties and restrictions set forth in the regulation.
